newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Low prices force S.African farmers to stock maize.
newsitem.headline: Low prices force S.African farmers to stock maize.

text.p: South Africa's National Maize Producers' Organisation (NAMPO) said on Monday it expected farmers to stockpile yellow maize from the current harvest due to low domestic prices.
NAMPO general manager Giel van Zyl told Reuters farmers were currently receiving offers of less than 500 rand a tonne, which did not cover producers' costs.
"Because farmers do not receive acceptable prices for yellow maize, I think lots of yellow would be retained as farmers' stock," van Zyl said.
He said many farmers who were currently busy harvesting would rather stockpile yellow maize than sell it at low prices.

Traders also said earlier this month that the continued weakness of the South African rand could see more yellow maize exported as farmers -- unhappy with low domestic prices -- aimed for better prices in export markets.
Van Zyl said the 1997 maize harvest was in full swing but the harvest would continue later than in previous years.

"The harvesting process is in full swing. In most areas of the country, farmers have made good progress with harvesting. It is clear that we will continue the harvest process into September as a result of the late harvest".
A normal crop would see harvesting being completed at the end of July.
South Africa expects a reduced crop this season, with the National Crop Estimates Committee's latest estimate at 7.966 million tonnes, sharply down on last season's bumper 9.69 million tonne crop.

Van Zyl and futures traders said fears of the effect of the El Nino weather phenomenon on South Africa's 1998 maize crop had already shown on maize contracts on the South African Futures Exchange (Safex).
Last week, Safex maize futures increased sharply on the back of a Chicago Board of Trade corn futures rally and perceptions of tight supply in the local market.
On Monday, yellow maize future contracts were sharply down across the board in early trading. The September contract was down nine rand at 545 rand from Friday's 554 settlement.
Traders said the slump could signal that the local market was following Chicago corn futures, which ended down on Friday.
But white maize futures held steady, with some increases in later-dated contracts.

"It is starting to sink in that there is a shortage of white maize in the country. With the fears of a possible El Nino next year which could affect production seriously, people are eager to protect their positions with physical stock and forward sales.
"I think we will see a similar situation in yellow maize. There is not as much yellow maize as everybody thinks," van Zyl said.
